TITLE: Investigating Optimal Brain Surgeon Framework for Sub-expert Pruning
PROPOSAL: We conduct a series of experiments on variably-sized MoE models, employing approximate Hessian estimation and iterative pruning with Optimal Brain Surgeon (OBS) framework to identify the most salient sub-expert units with minimal contribution to the overall performance. We analyze the trade-offs between various pruning ratios, hidden sizes, and pruning schemes (unit-wise, layer-wise).
CONTROLS: We compare the proposed approach to layer-wise Hessian estimation for pruning and single-expect-based pruning with OBS on matched-model setups.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (serving both pruned and large models, multiple iterations).
PREDICTION: Our approach significantly outperforms layer-wise Hessian-based pruning on sub-expert pruning, with considerable gains in pruning ratio for over 96\% of the parameters, while still delivering decent performance on smaller models, but may struggle to preserve accuracy with reduced pruning ratios (10-30\% of parameters) and may incur overfitting on various hyperparameter settings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Information-Theoretic Saliency for Sub-expert Pruning
PROPOSAL: We explore the application of information-theoretic metrics (KL-divergence, mutual information) to evaluate the importance of sub-expert units. In particular, we develop metrics that measure how much sub-expert units contribute to shaping the distribution of the output, allowing for a principled assessment of each unit's impact on overall performance.
CONTROLS: We compare against OBS, layer-wise Hessian estimation, and a baseline of random pruning.
COST: 200 GPU-hours (recomputing original runs with altered pruning criteria).
PREDICTION: Information-theoretic metrics tend to offer comparable or improved pruning results, as these methods directly evaluate the information transmitted to the downstream layers; however,KL-divergence may become unreliable for highly sparse and unbalanced sub-expert distributions.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Projection-based Regularization for Sub-expert Compressibility
PROPOSAL: We develop a novel method that imposes a low-dimensional projection constraint on each sub-expert layer, allowing us to identify units that contribute less to the overall expressiveness of the layer. Specifically, we compute the nominal-regularised eigen-value planes of sparse layers and transform them into matrices. We then perform a k-means clustering on the projected sub-expert matrices to identify units with similar patterns.
CONTROLS: Compare against OPTS, random pruning, and information-theoretic saliency metrics.
COST: 300 GPU-hours (increased k-means computation).
PREDICTION: Projection-based regularization offers a good compromise between pruning ratio and accuracy preservation, but performance may degrade on highly irregular sub-expert distributions due to the instability of k-means clustering.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Jointly Learning to Prune and Merge Sub-expert Units
PROPOSAL: We introduce an end-to-end pruning and merging framework that jointly optimizes the sub-expert units' importance scores and merging strategy. This framework enables the model to dynamically adjust the granularity of pruning based on the input data and task requirements, potentially achieving better trade-offs between pruning ratio and accuracy.
CONTROLS: Compare against existing expert-level pruning and merging methods, as well as the revised projection-based regularization approach.
COST: 800 GPU-hours (increased complexity of jointly learning pruning and merging).
PREDICTION: Our approach shows promising results, but may require extensive hyperparameter tuning to achieve optimal performance and stability.

ACTION: REVISE
TITLE: Investigating Optimal Brain Surgeon Framework for Sub-expert Pruning
PROPOSAL: We extend the Optimal Brain Surgeon (OBS) framework to handle sub-expert pruning by using a hierarchical approach. Specifically, we first prune the most important expert units using OBS, and then further prune the most important sub-expert units within each remaining expert, iteratively applying OBS to sub-expert layers.
CONTROLS: Compare against the revised projection-based regularization approach and jointly learning to prune and merge sub-expert units.
COST: 400 GPU-hours (added hierarchical pruning iterations).
PREDICTION: Hierarchical OBS pruning achieves state-of-the-art results, but may incur higher computational costs due to the nested pruning iterations; careful hyperparameter tuning is required to balance pruning ratio and accuracy preservation.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Evaluating Model Capacity and Limitations Under Pruning
PROPOSAL: We conduct a comprehensive study to evaluate the impact of sub-expert pruning on the theoretical capacity and limitations of MoE models. We use tools from information theory and statistical mechanics to analyze the effects of pruning on model expressiveness, information storage, and critical phenomena such as phase transitions.
CONTROLS: None, standalone theoretical analysis.
COST: 0 GPU-hours (theoretical analysis only).
PREDICTION: Our analysis reveals that sub-expert pruning has a more significant impact on model capacity than previously thought, particularly for deeper and wider models, and highlights the potential for phase transitions under heavy pruning.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Robustness Analysis of Pruned MoE Models
PROPOSAL: We perform a comprehensive robustness analysis of pruned MoE models to evaluate their resilience to various types of perturbations, including adversarial attacks, data corruption, and distributional shifts. We also investigate the effect of pruning on the robustness of MoE models and explore techniques to improve their robustness under pruning.
CONTROLS: Compare against the baseline MoE model and various pruning approaches.
COST: 600 GPU-hours (including data augmentation and perturbation simulations).
PREDICTION: Pruned MoE models exhibit poorer robustness compared to their full-size counterparts, but the jointly learned pruning and merging approach shows better robustness properties than other pruning methods.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Scalable Sub-expert Pruning for Large-Scale MoE Models
PROPOSAL: We develop a scalable and parallelizable sub-expert pruning algorithm for large-scale MoE models, leveraging recent advances in sparsification and parallelization techniques. Our approach allows for efficient pruning of massive MoE models on multiple GPUs and TPUs.
CONTROLS: Compare against existing pruning methods on large-scale MoE models.
COST: 1200 GPU-hours (including parallelization and distributed training).
PREDICTION: Our scalable sub-expert pruning algorithm significantly reduces pruning time and scales to large MoE models, while preserving accuracy and robustness.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Base-case Comparison of Expert Dropping and Merging Methods
PROPOSAL: Compare the performance of several state-of-the-art expert dropping and merging methods on realistic MoE models, applied to the C4 subset of the Stanford Question Answering Dataset (SQuAD v2.0) and evaluated using the Exact Match (EM) metric. We include baseline models, ablation experiments to evaluate the impact of different number of dropped or merged experts, as well as control experiments to compare the effect of different pruning hyperparameters.
CONTROLS: We compare against recent expert dropping methods, such as Adaptive Expert Pruning (AEP) and Channel Pruning (CP), as well as state-of-the-art expert merging methods like hard clustering and soft clustering (with different similarity measures).
COST: 100 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect to illustrate the existing trade-offs between accuracy, speedup, and model complexity in the existing expert dropping and merging methods, with fine-tuning required for many pruning configurations to maintain model performance. However, our findings could lay the groundwork for more detailed investigations into better pruning strategies.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Layer-wise Proportionality (Lp) and Its Impact on Expert Dropout
PROPOSAL: Develop and evaluate a layer-wise proportionality (Lp) criterion to assign more or less sparsity to different layers within MoE models. We analyze how varying Lp values affect expert dropout rates across layers and, consequently, overall model performance on SQuAD v2.0 and the GLUE benchmark suite. We also investigate the optimal Lp configuration for each task and evaluate its impact on speedup and memory reduction.
CONTROLS: Compare against existing expert dropping methods that rely on global calibration metrics, and conduct ablation experiments to assess the effect of varying Lp values and dataset splits.
COST: 150 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the Lp criterion will enable more fine-grained control over expert dropout, yielding better performance, but also introducing a new hyperparameter that needs to be tuned for optimal results.

ACTION: REVISE 2
TITLE: Layer-wise Proportionality (Lp) and Its Impact on Expert Dropout
PROPOSAL: Update Lp to dynamically adjust the proportion of active experts within each MoE layer based on the input sequence and layer output. Specifically, we introduce a contextual Lp (cLp) module that uses the input embedding and layer output to modulate the Lp value for each expert, allowing for adaptive sparse activation patterns. We evaluate cLp on SQuAD v2.0 and GLUE, comparing against the original Lp method and other state-of-the-art expert dropping approaches.
CONTROLS: Include ablation studies to understand cLp's performance when used in isolation, as well as with additional expert dropping methods, such as AEP and CP.
COST: 220 GPU-hours (increased due to the introduction of contextual information)
PREDICTION: We expect cLp to achieve better accuracy and speedup curves by adapting expert sparsity to the input context, but also introduce potential overhead due to additional computations.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Low-rank Decomposition for Expert Compression
PROPOSAL: Develop a low-rank decomposition (LRD) approach to compress expert weights within MoE models. Specifically, we factor each expert's weights into a product of a low-rank and a high-rank matrix, allowing for significant parameter reduction while preserving the original functionality. We apply LRD to several MoE models on SQuAD v2.0 and evaluate its performance using the Exact Match metric.
CONTROLS: Compare against existing expert merging and dropping methods, as well as baselines that simply reduce the expert weights by a fixed factor.
COST: 180 GPU-hours (dependent on the specific low-rank factorization algorithm used)
PREDICTION: We anticipate that LRD will yield efficient compression of expert weights, leading to notable memory savings and moderate performance drops on well-tuned MoE models.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Sub-Expert Importance Scores using Orthogonal Johnson Linguistics (OJL)
PROPOSAL: Introduce a novel method to estimate the importance of sub-expert units using Orthogonal Johnson Linguistics (OJL), a computationally efficient technique that preserves important weights and removes redundant orжу annotations. We apply OJL to estimate importance scores for individual sub-expert units and evaluate its effectiveness on SQuAD v2.0 and GLUE.
CONTROLS: Compare against existing methods for sub-expert importance estimation, such as the Optimal Brain Surgeon framework and first-order weight magnitudes.
COST: 80 GPU-hours
PREDICTION: We expect OJL to provide accurate importance estimates, allowing for more informed pruning decisions and potentially leading to better compressed models. However, its performance may degrade in extreme pruning settings.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Iterative Sub-Expert Pruning with Adaptive Regularization
PROPOSAL: Develop an iterative sub-expert pruning algorithm that adaptively adjusts the pruning schedule based on the estimated importance scores from OJL. We introduce a regularization term that encourages the removal of less important units, allowing for more aggressive pruning. We evaluate its performance on several MoE models on SQuAD v2.0 and GLUE, comparing against existing pruning methods.
CONTROLS: Compare against iterative pruning methods that rely on static pruning schedules, as well as those that use importance estimation but lack adaptive regularization.
COST: 250 GPU-hours (dependent on the number of pruning iterations)
PREDICTION: We anticipate that the iterative sub-expert pruning algorithm with adaptive regularization will yield better compression ratios and maintain model performance, but also potentially introduce additional optimization challenges.

ACTION: REVISE 3
TITLE: Low-rank Decomposition for Expert Compression
PROPOSAL: Update the low-rank decomposition (LRD) approach to consider the structural inductive bias of MoE models by incorporating the hierarchical organization of experts into the factorization process. Specifically, we propose a hierarchical low-rank decomposition (HLRD) that factorizes expert weights into a product of low-rank matrices capturing the interaction between experts at different layers. We apply HLRD to several MoE models on SQuAD v2.0 and evaluate its performance using the Exact Match metric.
CONTROLS: Compare against existing expert merging and dropping methods that ignore the hierarchical organization of experts, as well as the original LRD approach.
COST: 300 GPU-hours (dependent on the specific hierarchical factorization algorithm used)
PREDICTION: We expect HLRD to yield more efficient compression of expert weights by preserving the hierarchical relationships between experts, leading to improved model performance and reduced memory requirements. However, its computation may become more complex due to the additional layer-wise decomposition.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Expert Ensemble Learning for Sub-Expert Pruning
PROPOSAL: Develop an expert ensemble learning (EEL) method to select the most effective sub-expert units for pruning by learning to combine their predictions. We propose a novel neural network architecture that learns to weigh the contributions of individual sub-experts for each input sample, enabling selective pruning of less important sub-experts while preserving the overall model performance. We evaluate EEL on several MoE models on SQuAD v2.0 and GLUE, comparing against existing pruning methods.
CONTROLS: Compare against model-based pruning methods that rely on importance estimation, as well as sampling-based approaches that prune sub-experts uniformly.
COST: 320 GPU-hours (dependent on the size of the expert ensemble)
PREDICTION: We anticipate that EEL will yield better pruning results by selectively removing sub-experts that contribute less to the model's performance, leading to improved compression ratios and maintained model accuracy. However, its training process may become computationally expensive due to the need to learn the ensemble weights.

ACTION: ADD
TITLE: Quantifying the Impact of Sub-Expert Pruning on Model Uncertainty
PROPOSAL: Develop a method to quantify the impact of sub-expert pruning on the model's uncertainty, using tools from Bayesian deep learning to analyze the posterior distribution of the pruned model. We propose a technique to estimate the effect of sub-expert pruning on the model's variance and predictive distribution, enabling the selection of pruned models that balance compression and model uncertainty. We evaluate its performance on several MoE models on SQuAD v2.0 and GLUE, comparing against existing pruning methods.
CONTROLS: Compare against model-based pruning methods that ignore the impact of sub-expert pruning on model uncertainty, as well as sampling-based approaches that uniformly prune sub-experts.
COST: 380 GPU-hours (dependent on the computational complexity of estimating the posterior distribution)
PREDICTION: We anticipate that our method will provide a more complete understanding of the trade-off between compression and model uncertainty, enabling the selection of pruned models that balance these competing objectives. However, its computation may become more complex due to the need to estimate the posterior distribution.

ACTION: REVISE 1
TITLE: Base-case Comparison of Expert Dropping and Merging Methods
PROPOSAL: Update the base-case comparison study to include pruning methods that leverage sub-expert importance scores from Orthogonal Johnson Linguistics (OJL) and hierarchical low-rank decomposition (HLRD), as well as expert ensemble learning (EEL) for sub-expert pruning. We evaluate the performance of these methods on several MoE models on SQuAD v2.0 and GLUE, comparing against state-of-the-art pruning techniques and ablation studies to understand the contributions of each approach.
CONTROLS: Compare against a comprehensive set of pruning methods, including model-based, sampling-based, and ensemble-based approaches, as well as a range of pruning schedules and hyperparameters.
COST: 500 GPU-hours (dependent on the number of pruning methods and models evaluated)
PREDICTION: We expect this revised study to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the trade-offs between different pruning methods, highlighting the strengths and limitations of each approach and providing insights for future research directions.
